record.field: Run Payroll — your first pay run
Create one month of draft payslips for one division, and know exactly what you have and have not just done.
This screen creates a month of pay

Run Payroll takes one division and one period and computes a draft payslip for every eligible employee. Nothing is paid here — you are creating drafts to review. The four dots above tell you how far through that you are.

Picking a division here does more than filter a list of people: it selects the formula configuration every payslip in this run will be computed by. Retail's rules are not F&B's. Choose the wrong one and every number downstream is wrong in the same direction — the hardest kind of error to spot, because nothing looks odd.
The configuration name and its version are printed in the scope panel on the right. Read them before you compute, not after.

The period is the month being settled. The cycle is which part of it: mid-cycle pays an advance during the month, end-cycle settles the whole month. Most divisions run end-cycle only, which is why running the other one by accident produces a payslip that is not wrong so much as unexpected.
Read the eligible count before you compute

Payobook prints which configuration will run and how many employees are eligible. That count is your smoke alarm. If it says 12 where you expected 48, stop — the month's attendance import almost certainly has not been committed, and computing now would produce 12 real-looking payslips and 36 missing ones.
One press runs the formula configuration for every eligible employee: gross, allowances, BHXH/BHYT/BHTN, thuế TNCN, net. It takes seconds and it writes 48 draft records.

Affects July 2026 × Retail — Hà Nội only, 48 draft payslips. Reversible: yes — drafts can be recomputed or deleted, and nothing is paid or sent. No employee sees anything until the whole run reaches done. Verify first: the eligible count above, and that the month's import is committed.

Three numbers: how many payslips exist, how many computed cleanly, and how many the engine wants a human to look at. That third one is Need review, and it is not an error count. A flag is the engine saying it found something unusual and would like you to confirm it is intended.
One flag, and why it is not an error

Trần Văn Hùng's overtime is 4,200,000 ₫ against 1,100,000 ₫ in June — 382% of last month. That may be perfectly correct: a shop refit, a peak week, a genuine burst. It may also be 4.6 hours typed as 46. The engine cannot tell those apart and does not pretend to; you can, by checking the timesheet.
A flag you clear without understanding is a flag you have answered with a guess.

The run is now in draft on the Pay Runs board. From here it travels through the Payroll Officer tier, {{hrTierName}}, {{gmTierName}} and then done. Each gate belongs to one group; nobody can skip one, and a rejection at any of them returns the run to draft with a written reason.
You computed July for Retail and then spot that one employee's overtime input is wrong. What is the safest next step?
Edit the net amount directly on the payslip

Let's rethink that. Editing the output breaks the trail: the slip no longer agrees with the data behind it, and the next recompute silently undoes your fix — so the mistake comes back without anyone touching it.
Fix the overtime input, then recompute the draft
Exactly. Drafts exist for this: correct the input, recompute, and every dependent line — gross, thuế TNCN, net — corrects itself, because they were all derived from that input in the first place.
Submit for approval now and correct it next month
Let's rethink that. It turns a thirty-second fix into a retro line next month — and an employee who was paid the wrong amount today, which is the part they will remember.
Read the Pay Runs board the way payroll week needs it read: what is stuck, whose gate it is stuck at, and what a rejection actually does.
Five numbers, and only one of them is yours

Total runs, in pipeline, awaiting your approval, completed, net paid. Four of those describe the department. The third one describes you: it is the work that will not move until you move it, and it is the number to read first every morning of payroll week.
The columns are stages, not months

This is the single most common misreading of this screen. A column is an approval stage, so July and June can sit side by side in the same one, and a run moves left to right by being approved — never by being edited. Use the date chips below when you want a period.

Five stages, in that order, every time. Each gate belongs to one group, so the chain is also an answer to 'who do I chase': the run's current column names the person. Nothing skips a gate — not for a deadline, not for a director.
A card only offers what you can actually do

The buttons on a card are decided by the record's own gate fields and your groups — not by the card. If you cannot see Approve here, you do not hold that tier, and pressing harder will not help. That is also why the same run shows different buttons to different people.
A rejection is testimony, not a rebuke

Rejecting sends the whole run back to draft and records three things against it: who rejected it, when, and why in writing. That written reason is the entire value of the rejection. Without it the officer who has to fix the run is guessing at what you saw, and will probably resubmit the same thing.

Affects the whole run, not one payslip: all 48 return to draft together. Reversible: yes — it is recomputed and resubmitted through the same chain, and nothing was paid. Verify first: that the problem really is the run, and not a single slip you could have discussed.
Every count above is scoped by these chips

The KPI band is not the whole database — it is whatever the active date chip and division chip allow through. A number that looks alarming is worth re-reading with the scope in mind before it becomes an email.
Done unlocks the money, and locks the run

Only a completed run offers {{bankFileFormat}}, the journals and the payments. That is the point of the chain — those buttons appear exactly when every gate has said yes. It is also the last reversible moment: after done, a correction is a retro line, never an edit.
A run has been sitting at {{hrTierName}} for two days and payday is on {{payDay}}. You are the Payroll Officer. What do you do?
Recompute the run so it moves forward
Let's rethink that. Recomputing does not move a run through a gate — approving does. It would also change figures the reviewer has already read, so they would have to start again.
Ask the person who holds that tier — the column names them

Yes. The column a run is sitting in is the answer to who can move it. Chasing the right person is the only thing that shortens the wait, and it is also the fastest way to find out whether they are stuck on something you can resolve.
Reject it yourself and start a clean run
Let's rethink that. A rejection is testimony about a problem you found — using it as a scheduling tool puts a reason on the record that is not true, and throws away two days of somebody's review.
Read a payslip like an auditor
Take one payslip apart line by line and be able to say, out loud, where every number came from.
Everything below belongs to one run
The selector at the top names the run. Every KPI, every chip and every slip under it is scoped to that run — so comparing two months means changing this control, not scrolling.

Forty-eight slips is more than anyone reads carefully. The engine has already told you which ones it could not settle on its own — start there, and sample a few of the rest. Reading top to bottom is how a flagged slip gets approved at 6pm.
A payslip carries its own position
The stepper here is this slip's stage, which is not always the run's. That distinction matters when a single payslip has been pulled out for a question while the rest of the batch moved on.
Gross to net, one line at a time

Mai's July: base 12,000,000 plus allowances 780,000 plus overtime 1,500,000 is a gross of 14,280,000 ₫. Then BHXH 960,000, BHYT 180,000, BHTN 120,000 and thuế TNCN 101,000 come off, leaving 12,919,000 ₫. Every one of those is a named rule, not a typed number.
Insurance is not charged on what you earned

BHXH, BHYT and BHTN are charged on the registered insurance base — for Mai, 12,000,000 ₫, her contract base. Not on gross. That is why 1,500,000 ₫ of overtime moved her tax and did not move her insurance by a single đồng, and it answers most variance questions before they are asked.
Say it as a sentence: insurance follows the contract, tax follows the month.

Toggle between June and July and watch which lines move. Overtime and thuế TNCN move; insurance does not. Once you can predict which lines will move before you look, you can review forty-eight payslips in the time it used to take to explain one.
Net is 855,000 ₫ higher. Overtime rose 900,000 and PIT took 45,000 of it. Insurance is identical, because it is charged on the registered base and overtime does not touch that.
An employee's overtime doubled this month but their BHXH deduction is unchanged. What is the correct reading?
The insurance calculation is broken and should be reported

Let's rethink that. It is working exactly as the law describes: contributions are charged on the registered base, and overtime is not part of that base. Reporting it would send someone looking for a bug that is not there.
Correct — insurance is charged on the registered base, which overtime does not change

Yes. Insurance follows the contract, tax follows the month. This is the single fact that explains most of the variance questions a payroll desk receives, and being able to say it plainly is worth more than any report.
Their insurance base should be raised to match the higher earnings

Let's rethink that. The registered base is a declared contract figure, not something payroll adjusts to follow a busy month — changing it is an HR and legal decision with consequences well beyond this payslip.
Get a month of attendance and overtime into Payobook, and know exactly what the confidence score is telling you before you commit.
Map, validate, commit — and only the last one writes

Three stages, and a batch that stops before the last one has changed nothing at all. That is the whole design: you are allowed to load a bad file, look at it, and walk away, and the system is exactly as it was.
The other import surfaces exist for specific tools and older habits. This one scores the file before it writes, which is the difference between finding a bad row now and finding it on {{payDay}}.

It is not a grade. It is the share of rows the importer could match to an employee and read without ambiguity: 46 of 48. 95.8% of 48 rows still leaves two rows that need a human — and those two are the ones that become a missing or a wrong payslip.
Match, Retry or Skip — and Skip has a cost

Match points a row at the right employee. Retry re-reads it after you correct the file. Skip drops it — which is legitimate for a duplicate row and quietly wrong for an employee, because a skipped employee is simply absent from the run.
Skipping a duplicate and skipping a person look identical on this screen. The difference is entirely in what you understood about the row.
Commit is the first thing here that writes
Everything before this was a preview. Pressing it writes the rows into the period and they become the inputs the next compute reads.

Affects the period this batch names, for every row it holds. Reversible: partly — you can import a correction, but rows already read into a computed run leave payslips that must be recomputed. Verify first: the period on the batch, that Need attention is zero, and that every Skip you used was a duplicate and not a person.
Never fix an import on the payslips

It is tempting: the payslip is right in front of you and the number is obviously wrong. But editing here corrects the output and leaves the input untouched, so the next recompute brings the mistake straight back — and now the slip and the timesheet disagree, which is worse than the original error.
The confidence score is 91%, five rows need attention, and the import cut-off is {{importCutoff}}. What do you do?
Commit — 91% is high enough and the deadline is today
Let's rethink that. The score is not a pass mark; the five rows are five people. Committing now means five payslips that are missing or wrong, discovered by the employees rather than by you.
Resolve the five rows first, then commit
Yes. Each of those rows is a person who would otherwise be absent from the run or paid on the wrong figure — and every one of them is cheaper to fix now than as a retro line next month.
Skip the five rows so the score reaches 100%
Let's rethink that. Skipping removes the rows from the batch, not the problem from the month — the score goes green because those people are no longer in the import at all.
Read a division's rulebook end to end, and be able to point at the component that produced any line on a payslip.

This is HOASEN_RETAIL_END — the configuration every Retail payslip is computed by. The name at the top is a switcher: other divisions have their own, and they are not variations of this one. Choosing a division in Run Payroll is choosing which of these runs.

The code is the thing to quote when you ask someone about a number: "HOASEN_RETAIL_END, component TNCN" is a question that can be answered. The shape is PREFIX_DIVISION_CYCLE and the prefix belongs to the company — this practice company uses HOASEN, the Payobook demo world uses DEMO. Learn the shape, not the prefix.
Every line on a payslip is a component here

Ten components in four kinds — inputs (base salary), earnings (allowances, overtime), deductions (BHXH, BHYT, BHTN, thuế TNCN) and totals (gross, taxable, net) — and below them the parameters those formulas reference. Nothing on a payslip comes from anywhere else: if a line exists it is one of these, and if a line is wrong the number behind it is one of these too.
EESI, EEHI and EEUI are the contribution rates, and they live HERE — on the configuration. The Statutory screen declares what the company contributes; this is what actually charges it.
Read it out loud and it is just a sentence

TNCN = 5% × TNCT, and TNCT = GROSS − (BHXH + BHYT + BHTN) − 11,000,000. That is the whole of Mai's tax line: gross, less her insurance, less the personal deduction, then the first band's rate. Each coloured chip is a component you can click through to.
The 11,000,000 is written as a chip, not typed into the formula twice. One relief figure, one place to change it.
Names for people, letters for spreadsheets

The same formula switches between Names (TNCN = 5% × TNCT) and Letters (I = 5% × H). Letters are how the engine stores it and how it reads next to a spreadsheet; names are how you explain it to somebody. They are one formula in two spellings, so a change in either is a change in both.

TNCT depends on GROSS, BHXH, BHYT and BHTN — change any of those and it moves. It is used by THUCNHAN, so the net follows it. This panel is the one to read before renaming or deleting anything: it names, exactly, what would break.
The rulebook, run on a real person

The preview evaluates the whole configuration against one employee: Mai's gross of 14,280,000 ₫, taxable of 2,020,000, tax of 101,000 and net of 12,919,000 ₫. This is the same arithmetic her payslip shows — the difference is that here you can see which component produced each line.

Simulate runs the edited configuration against a period that has already been paid, and shows you what would have come out. It is the only way to see a change's effect on people rather than on one preview employee — and it costs a minute.

Affects every future payslip computed by this configuration — the whole division, not one employee, and not one month. Reversible: partly — the configuration can be edited back, but any run already computed on the changed version keeps its figures until it is recomputed. Verify first: the dependency panel for anything you renamed, and a simulation against last month.
You need to add a meal allowance for Retail. The July run is computed and waiting at {{hrTierName}}. What do you do?
Add the component now — the July run has already been computed, so it cannot be affected

Let's rethink that. Computed is not finished: a rejection at any gate sends the run back to draft, and the recompute that follows would use the configuration as it is then — so July would quietly acquire an allowance that was never approved for it.
Add the component, simulate it against last month, and apply it once July is done

Yes. The simulation tells you what the change does to real people before anybody is paid by it, and waiting for July to reach done means no open run can pick it up by accident. Both halves matter — the simulation is the evidence, the timing is the safety.
Add the allowance straight onto each employee's payslip instead

Let's rethink that. That is forty-eight manual edits that the next recompute erases, and next month it is forty-eight more. A component is written once and paid every month; an edit is written every month and remembered by nobody.
Statutory — the rules the law writes
Read the policy and the tax table the way an inspector would, and know exactly how to apply a rate change without touching a month that is already open.
You do not invent these numbers

This screen holds what the law has already decided: the BHXH, BHYT and BHTN rates, the base they are charged on, and the thuế TNCN table. Your job is not to choose them — it is to keep them current, and to be able to show where each one came from.
Who pays what — and the bigger half is not yours

Each scheme has an employee share, deducted from the payslip, and an employer share, which is a company cost and never appears in anybody's net. BHXH 8% / 17.5% · BHYT 1.5% / 3% · BHTN 1% / 1%. The employee pays 10.5% in total and the company pays 21.5% — twice as much, on top.
When an employee says "I pay a third of my salary in insurance", this table is the answer: they pay 10.5% of the registered base, and the company pays the rest.
Charged on the registered base, up to a ceiling

Contributions apply to the registered insurance base — for Mai, her contract base of 12,000,000 ₫, not her 14,280,000 ₫ gross. And they stop at the ceiling in the last column: above 20,000,000 ₫ the deduction does not grow, so two people on very different salaries can pay exactly the same BHXH.
PIT is progressive, and kind at the bottom

Taxable income is gross less insurance, less 11,000,000 ₫ for yourself and 4,400,000 ₫ per dependant. Mai: 14,280,000 − 1,260,000 − 11,000,000 = 2,020,000 ₫, which sits entirely in the 5% band, so her tax is 101,000 ₫. The bands only bite further up.
Insurance comes off BEFORE the deductions, which is why a rise in a contribution rate always costs a little less net than it costs in contribution.
Check the declared rate against the charged one

The 1.5% on the BHYT row is what the company declares. The −180,000 ₫ on Mai's July slip is what her division's configuration actually charged — 1.5% of her registered base of 12,000,000 ₫. Today they agree, and this line is how you check that. They are two records, though: editing the rate here would not move that đồng by itself.
The number that priced that line is a parameter on Retail's configuration — EEHI, at the bottom of the component list in Formula Engine. That is where a rate actually moves a payslip.
A rate change is a new record, not an edit

There is no version history on a policy. When a decree changes a rate you create a new policy record with its own code — codes are unique per company — and its own effective date. The old record stays as the evidence of what was declared before it; archiving it takes it off this list, which is why the roster shows the live declarations rather than the whole history.

The rates table above shows the ACTIVE policy with the latest effective date. It does not compare that date to today and it does not read the end date — so a policy dated from next month is displayed the moment it is saved.
Declaring a rate is half the job

Saving a new policy changes what this screen, the contribution analytics and the statutory reports say. It changes no payslip. The rate that prices pay is a parameter on each division's formula configuration, so a rate change is two pieces of work: declare it here, and change it there. Until both are done the two disagree — and it is this screen, not the payslip, that is telling the truth about the company's intention.

Affects what is declared and reported, company-wide: this cockpit, the contribution analytics and the statutory reports. It does not reprice a single payslip on its own. Reversible: yes — archive the record and the previous declaration is displayed again, because nothing downstream has been recomputed from it. Verify first: that you know which configurations have to change too, and who is going to change them.
What half a percentage point costs

If BHYT's employee share went from 1.5% to 2.0%, Mai's deduction grows 60,000 ₫ — and her net falls 57,000 ₫, not 60,000, because insurance comes off before tax and her thuế TNCN falls 3,000 with it. Toggle the two sides and read which lines move.

Net falls 57,000 ₫, not 60,000. The deduction grew by 60,000, and because insurance comes off before tax, taxable income fell by the same 60,000 and PIT fell 3,000 with it. Half a percentage point, one employee, every month.
A decree raises BHYT's employee share from 1 August. It is 20 July and the July run is still awaiting {{gmTierName}}. What do you do?
Edit the rate on the policy that is in force now

Let's rethink that. There is no version history to fall back on — the old declared rate is simply gone, and with it the record of what the company was declaring while July was being paid. That record is exactly what an inspection asks to see.
Create a new policy record dated 01/08, and plan the configuration change with it

Yes. The date records what the decree says, the old record stays as evidence of what was declared before it, and — the half people forget — the rate that actually prices pay is a parameter on each division's configuration, so somebody has to change that too before August runs.
Create the new policy now with today's date so nothing is forgotten

Let's rethink that. The instinct is right and the date is wrong: today means 20 July, and the decree does not say 20 July — so the declaration would record a legal start the company cannot evidence. Create the record now if you like; put 01/08 in the effective date, and tell whoever is reviewing July that the rates on this screen are next month's.
Decide on a run the way somebody who will be asked about it decides: flags first, a sample after, and a variance you can explain in one sentence before you sign.
This screen is a queue, not a board

The Pay Runs board shows every run there is. This one shows only the runs a human still has to answer for — and the chip in the corner counts the ones waiting on you. Everything else here is somebody else's signature, shown so you know who to ask rather than so you can do it for them.
Net at stake is money that has not been paid yet

Three counts, one per gate, and then 612,480,000 ₫ — the net of every run in the pipeline. It is worth reading as what it is: money that is one or more signatures away from leaving the company's account, and that can still be stopped by anybody who finds a reason to.
After the last gate that sentence stops being true. A correction to a completed run is a retro line in the next one, never an edit to this one.
A lane is a gate, and an empty one is not a fault

Officer review, then {{hrTierName}}, then {{gmTierName}}. A run sits in the lane of the gate it is waiting at, so the lane names the person to chase. Two of the three are empty here, and that is what most days look like — a lane fills when work reaches it and empties when somebody signs.
A card offers Approve and Reject only at the gate you hold. If you cannot see them, you are looking at somebody else's work, and pressing harder will not help.
Nobody reads forty-eight payslips, and nobody should

Reading top to bottom is how a flagged payslip gets approved at six in the evening. The engine has already told you which ones it could not settle on its own — start there, then sample two or three it did not flag. A flag marks the unusual, not the wrong, so a clean slip can still be incorrect and a flagged one can be perfectly fine.
Sampling is not a shortcut. It is how you find out whether the flags are the only problem — and if a sampled slip is wrong, the flags were never the point.
Explain the variance, or you are not ready to sign

July is 612,480,000 ₫ against June's 596,110,000 ₫. Toggle the two and say, out loud, why they differ — one more employee, and one payslip with 3,100,000 ₫ more overtime on it than last month. If you cannot finish that sentence, the gap is not small; it is unexamined.
48 employees · one payslip flagged, still unanswered

16,370,000 ₫ more, which is 2.7% on one extra employee. That is a comfortable-looking number, and comfortable-looking numbers are where a single wrong payslip hides best: Hùng's 3,100,000 ₫ of extra overtime sits inside it, and nothing about the total says so.
A rejection is testimony, and the reason is required

Rejecting sends the whole run back to draft — all 48 payslips together, never one — and records three things against it: who rejected it, when, and why in writing. The product requires that reason because without it the officer who has to fix the run is guessing at what you saw, and will probably resubmit the same thing.
"Payslip NV0031 — overtime is 382% of June, verify against the timesheet" is a reason somebody can act on. "Wrong" is a reason somebody has to interpret.
Approving is a signature, and it moves real money

Nothing about the button says so, which is why this step does. Pressing Approve moves 48 payslips one gate closer to being paid, together — there is no way to approve some of them — and the gate after yours checks totals rather than lines. If a wrong line is going to be caught, this is one of the last places it can be.

Affects the whole run, all 48 payslips together. It moves from your gate to the next one. Reversible: yes, for now — a later reviewer can still reject it back to draft, and that stops being true at done, after which a correction is a retro line. Verify first: every flagged payslip opened, a few unflagged ones sampled, and a one-sentence explanation of the variance against last month.
Whatever you decide is written down with your name on it

Approvals and rejections land in the same list, and a rejection keeps its written reason where the next person can read it. That is not surveillance — it is the reason a payroll month can be defended six months later, when nobody remembers the conversation and the record is all there is.
A run is waiting at your gate. The total is 2.7% above last month, one payslip is flagged and nobody has opened it, and payday is {{payDay}}. What do you do?
Approve — 2.7% against last month is well within normal

Let's rethink that. A total that looks reasonable is not evidence that every slip inside it is: one payslip with 3,100,000 ₫ of extra overtime sits comfortably inside a 2.7% move. The flag was raised about one employee, and approving without opening it is answering that question with silence.
Open the flagged payslip, and decide once you can say in one sentence why the total moved

Yes. That sentence is the whole test, and it takes minutes: one more employee, and one payslip with far more overtime than last month. Once you can say it you can approve with your eyes open — or reject with something the officer can act on.
Reject it so the officer re-checks everything before payday

Let's rethink that. Rejecting sends all 48 payslips back to draft and puts a reason on the permanent record — and "please check everything" is not a reason anybody can act on. A rejection is testimony about a problem you found, not a way of asking somebody to go looking for one.
Read the Dashboard the way the first ten minutes of a payroll day needs it read — and know where everything else in Payobook lives.
The state of payroll, before you choose anything

This is the one screen that answers "where is payroll right now" without a filter, a period or a division being picked first. The line under your name is the live run: which one it is, how many payslips it holds, and how many are still waiting on a signature.
Read it before your inbox. An email about payroll is somebody's version of this line; this is the line.
Four numbers, and only one of them is a queue

Headcount, monthly payroll, pending approval, active configurations. Three of those describe the company and will read almost the same tomorrow. Pending approval is different: it is work that has stopped, and it is the only number here that somebody has to do something about.
It counts the company's pending sign-offs, at every gate — not yours. How many are yours is a question the Approvals screen answers.
Pay is computed from a rulebook you can read

Payobook does not hide its arithmetic behind fixed salary structures. Every line on every payslip comes from a named component in a formula configuration — one per division — written the way a spreadsheet is written and readable by the person who has to explain it. This card is the way in; the Formula Engine lesson is where you take one apart.
That is why "why is my pay this number" has an answer here rather than a promise to look into it.
Nothing on this screen is a second way of doing anything

The buttons and cards here open the same screens the sidebar opens. Run Payroll from the hero is the same wizard as the Run Payroll leaf — same rules, same gates, same consequences. A dashboard that had its own shortcut to computing a run would be a second place for a run to be created, and there would be no way to be sure which one made the month.
Payroll is a loop, not a task

Each row here is one month that was imported, computed, reviewed, approved by every gate and paid. The same loop, every month, in the same order — and the reason a run has a state rather than a tick is that the loop can stop at any point in it and somebody has to know where.
Six sections, and you only work in two of them

Overview is where you land and where approvals queue. Pay Run is the month's work, top to bottom. People holds who can be paid, Insights answers questions about what was paid, and Setup is read often and changed rarely. A leaf that is not in your sidebar is one your groups do not open — the Journey still describes it, because the person who cannot open a screen is exactly the person who needs to know what it is.
The Learning section is this one. Everything you are reading now lives there, and it stays there while you work.
There is a Coach on every screen, and it will not act for you

The launcher in the bottom-right corner opens on any screen in Payobook, and it answers about the screen you are standing on: what it is, what to do next here, what a tile counts, and what a control would do before you press it. It guides — you act. It never computes a run, approves a payslip or changes a record, and it never invents a rate: every answer it gives is something a person wrote and a test checks.
If it has nothing written for a screen it says so. "I do not have lessons for this screen yet" is a better answer than a confident one about the wrong screen.
The Dashboard says 3 pending approval. You hold the {{hrTierName}} gate. What does that number tell you about your own morning?
Three runs are waiting for my signature

Let's rethink that. The tile counts every sign-off the company is waiting on, at every gate — most of them belong to somebody else. Acting on it as a personal queue means chasing runs that were never yours and missing the ones that were.
Three runs are waiting for somebody's signature, and Approvals will tell me how many are mine

Exactly. The Dashboard reports the state; the queue that is yours has its own screen, and its header counts only what your groups let you act on. Reading the state first and the queue second is the order the whole product is built in.

Let's rethink that. Runs sitting at a gate mid-month is what a working approval chain looks like — the number only means "behind" once you know which gate each one is at and how long it has been there, and neither of those is on this tile.
